newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECHS HOPE GERMAN PACT HELPS SEAL NATO, EU DRIVE.
newsitem.headline: CZECHS HOPE GERMAN PACT HELPS SEAL NATO, EU DRIVE.

text.p: Czech officials hope that the completion of a joint post-World War Two act of contrition with Germany will give fresh impetus to Prague's drive to join NATO and the European Union, a senior diplomat said on Wednesday.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl is due in Prague on January 21 and 22 to sign the reconciliation accord in which Bonn expresses its sorrow for the 1938-45 Nazi occupation of the Czech lands and Prague its regret for Czech brutality in the post-war expulsion of ethnic Germans.

The text, which deals mostly with tying up loose ends of the neighbouring countries' harrowing past, also includes Germany's full backing for the Czechs to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) and the EU.

Although Bonn has often given verbal support for Czech membership in western organisations since the fall of communism in 1989, the diplomat said that the declaration would give new gravity to Bonn's words.

"When you have the Germans actually write something down, it is an important obligation for them, their support for the Czechs is an important matter," said the senior Czech diplomat, who asked not to be named.
The diplomat also said the Czech-German agreement, initialled in December after two years of sensitive negotiations, was under close scrutiny in other countries.
"Germany has been watched closely in the process by its neighbours... There is historical distrust of (Germany)," the diplomat said.

The Czech Republic is the last of Germany's neighbours not to have signed a post-war reconciliation agreement, as lingering issues over compensation for the Nazi occupation, and the Czech seizure of ethnic German property have remained open.

"If there was not such a document, it would have been a complication not only for the Czechs, but for the whole Union," the diplomat said. "As I see it, the Union also feels relieved that it is behind us."

In the agreement, Bonn and Prague set up a 160 million mark "Future Fund" mostly with German contributions, to finance joint outreach projects, but it is mainly aimed at helping victims of Nazi aggression.

The deal has been roundly criticised by families and supporters of expelled Sudeten Germans -- mostly living now in the southern state of Bavaria -- because there is no direct compensation provided for property taken by Czechs in the war's aftermath.
